newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flatulent livestock cause EU methane problem.
newsitem.headline: Flatulent livestock cause EU methane problem.

text.p: Flatulent sheep and cows and their decomposing manure account for 10 million tonnes, or nearly half, of the EU's annual emissions of methane, a gas second only to carbon dioxide (CO2) for its effect on global climate change.
The revelation is contained in a strategy paper adopted by the European Commission on Tuesday, which includes policy ideas to cut EU methane emissions by 41 percent of 1990 levels by 2010.
Under existing policies, emissions are slated to drop by 14.3 percent of 1990 levels during the same period.
"Methane is the second most important greenhouse gas, after CO2, and accounts for nearly one fifth of the global greenhouse effect," the Commission said in a statement.
"Being an active gas, it traps heat and inhibits its release into space, increasing atmospheric and earth-surface temperatures," it added.
United Nations climate scientists have said greenhouse gases from human actions have a discernible influence on global climate, although opinion is split on their exact effects.

While livestock generates 44.7 percent of the EU's methane emissions, according to 1990 figures, waste accounts for 31.5 percent with a further 23 percent coming from energy-related activities such as coal mining and gas production and distribution.

In relation to farm-generated methane, the paper skirts the issue of cutting EU herds or boosting animals' capacity to grow quicker or to produce more milk, preferring instead to concentrate on developing the technologies for creating manure lagoons and digesters with methane collection or flare off.
For rubbish tips, the paper moots the idea of rules to cut organic waste production, to equip existing dumps with recovery or flare-off systems and to make these mandatory for new dumps.
For coal mining, a sector in decline across the 15-country bloc, the Commission said additional measures to curb methane emissions would be "extremely difficult to justify".
The Commission paper is intended to spark off discussions ahead of any legislative proposals.
